summary:
First and Second Kings were originally a single book, divided in two by its Greek translators. Together they run from David's last days (about 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, grading every reign with a refrain: each king "did evil in the sight of the LORD" or "did what was right in the eyes of the LORD." It opens with a contest for the dying David's throne: Adonijah, the eldest surviving son, claims it, but Nathan the prophet (a prophet speaks for God) and Bathsheba win it for Solomon. At Gibeon God offers him whatever he asks; Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil" (3:9), and is tested at once: two mothers claim one baby, and Solomon finds the real one by offering to divide him with a sword (3:16–28).

Chapters 6–8 build the temple in Jerusalem — "So he built the temple in seven years" (6:38). At its dedication a cloud fills the house, and Solomon's prayer asks, "But will God indeed dwell upon the earth? The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You" (8:27). Wisdom and wealth draw the queen of Sheba (ch. 10); chapter 11 turns. Seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines "turned his heart after other gods" — Ashtoreth, Chemosh, Milcom, the gods of neighboring nations — and the prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak into twelve pieces and hands ten to the official Jeroboam: the kingdom will be torn from Solomon's son, one tribe kept "for the sake of My servant David" (11:32).

Solomon's son Rehoboam then meets a plea to lighten the kingdom's forced labor with threats of worse (12:14), and ten northern tribes secede under Jeroboam — Israel in the north, Judah under David's line in Jerusalem. To keep pilgrims from returning to the Jerusalem temple, Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan — "Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (12:28), nearly Aaron's words at Sinai (Exodus 32:4) — and Jeroboam's sin becomes the charge against every northern king after him. Israel's throne then passes by assassination until Omri builds a new capital, Samaria (16:24); his son Ahab marries Jezebel of Sidon and builds a temple there for Baal, the Canaanite storm god.

The final third belongs to the prophet Elijah. He announces a drought — "neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!" (17:1) — and is fed by ravens, then by a widow in Zarephath of Sidon whose flour and oil do not run out (Jesus points to her in Luke 4:25–26). On Mount Carmel he faces 450 prophets of Baal: "If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him" (18:21). Fire from the LORD consumes the water-drenched offering, and the people fall facedown: "The LORD, He is God!" (18:39). Fleeing Jezebel's death threat, Elijah reaches Horeb, where the law was given (Deuteronomy 5:2): wind, earthquake, and fire pass, the LORD in none of them, and then comes "a still, small voice" (19:12). The book closes on Ahab's house: Jezebel has Naboth killed on false charges to seize his vineyard (ch. 21), Micaiah son of Imlah stands alone against four hundred court prophets, and Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead, struck by an archer who "drew his bow without taking special aim" (ch. 22); the account runs straight on into 2 Kings.
